ManipulaXIntel Physical AI Challenge · simulation-first

Two arms, one dinner table, one sentence of instruction.

Dual SO-ARM100 manipulators in MuJoCo open a drawer, pass a fork between arms, and lay a place setting — driven by a language-conditioned policy compiled to OpenVINO and measured on an Intel Core Ultra 7.

What the two arms actually have to share

The cutlery drawer sits on the left; the fork belongs on the right of the mat. Each arm reaches a band roughly 0.11–0.30 m from its own base, and neither band covers both. The hand-off is not decoration — the layout makes it the only way to finish. The second coordination moment is the pour: one arm holds the mug in the air while the other tips the bottle into it.

Every seed, every sub-task

Ten randomised seeds at full domain randomisation — object shape, mass, friction, placement, lighting, background and camera pose all redrawn per seed. One cell per seed, so the pattern is visible rather than averaged away.

Sub-taskArmSeeds 0–9Rate

Mug on the mat left 3/10
Pour into the mug both 0/10

completenot complete

The drawer is solid across all ten, and the plate lands in eight. The hand-off carries six, and it is verified rather than assumed — the receiving arm has to genuinely have the fork between its fingers or the transfer is refused.

The pour is the one that does not land. The bottle tips and releases, but the stream begins while the spout is still short of the mug, so no episode completes all six. It is reported here as measured.

All three Intel devices, measured

The policy is a 1.01 M-parameter action-chunk transformer exported to OpenVINO IR and swept across every device and precision the Core Ultra 7 155H offers.

The CPU wins, by roughly 23× over the NPU — and that is the finding. A model this small on three 96×96 images cannot amortise dispatch overhead on an accelerator, so fixed per-inference cost dominates: the NPU comes in slower than unoptimised PyTorch. Offloading to an NPU is a win for sustained large models, and this policy is deliberately neither.

One inference yields a 16-step action chunk, so INT8 sustains about 18,083 Hz of control against a 30 Hz requirement. Latency was never the binding constraint.

Quantisation, and a result worth flagging

Deviation from the PyTorch reference on held-out demonstration frames, as a share of the output's own standard deviation — the scale-free reading.

7.6%INT8 drift · 1.2 MB
45.9%FP16 drift · 1.95 MB

Calibrated INT8 is both smaller and more faithful than naive FP16. The difference is calibration: post-training quantisation saw real recorded frames and joint states and placed its ranges accordingly, while FP16 rounds every weight blindly — and a two-layer pre-norm transformer at d_model 128 has little headroom for that. FP16 is not automatically the safe default.

How it is put together

Hierarchical, because a single end-to-end model driving a ten-step sequence — trained without a GPU and without teleoperation data — does not work. Each tier does what it is good at.

Planner

Sentence plus the overhead camera into a JSON plan, schema-validated and repaired, with a deterministic planner behind it when the model's output fails validation.

SmolVLM-500M · INT8
Coordinator

Arm assignment, the hand-off state machine, shared-workspace sequencing, and a replan against the current scene whenever a sub-task fails.

per sub-task
Policy

Three camera views and 24-D proprioception with the active sub-task as a language token, emitting a 16-step × 12-DoF action chunk.
